subsection: 4. How the global economy is organised

notes.b: A basic processing unit is a factory carrying out one stage of production: processing a raw material, making a component or assembling a product. Multinational companies (MNCs) place each stage in whichever country suits it best.
points: The Intel and Apple chains, described in the note 'One multinational company (MNC)', are examples of stages spread across several countries.
Cheap labour suits labour-intensive assembly.
Units are placed close to raw materials or to markets.
A factory inside a trade bloc sells to the bloc's members without the barriers that apply to imports from outside.
Tax breaks and grants lower the cost of operating in a country.
Falling transport and communication costs make distant factories practical.
Spreading production across many countries means that one disaster or strike does not stop all production.

notes.b: Nike designs and sells shoes but owns almost none of the factories that make them.
points: Founded as Blue Ribbon Sports in 1964 by Phil Knight and Bill Bowerman; renamed Nike in 1971.
Headquarters, design and marketing are in Beaverton, Oregon, USA.
Footwear is made by independent contract factories, mainly in Vietnam (the largest), China and Indonesia.
Nike sells its products worldwide.
Sweatshop criticism in the 1990s, including of factories in Indonesia, led to factory monitoring and published supplier lists.

notes.h: Export processing zones (EPZs) and Special Economic Zones
notes.b: In an export processing zone, firms import components and export finished goods free of customs duty, and they receive tax breaks.
points: Shannon Free Zone, Co. Clare, set up in 1959, was one of the world's first export processing zones and Ireland's pioneer.
Shenzhen, China, became a Special Economic Zone in 1980.
Maquiladoras are assembly plants along Mexico's border with the USA, such as those at Tijuana and Ciudad Juárez, set up from 1965.
A maquiladora imports components duty-free and exports finished goods to the USA.
Long supply chains are vulnerable to disruption, as the 2021 chip shortage, the Ever Given blockage and the Red Sea diversions showed (see the note 'Patterns in world trade').
Branch plants close when costs change, and their workers lose jobs.
Some plants pay low wages and have poor conditions.
Moving components and goods over long distances has an environmental cost.
Responses include reshoring (moving production back to the home country) and friend-shoring (moving it to politically allied countries).
Core regions have capital, MNC headquarters, research and development, skilled labour, good infrastructure and political power.
The core's examples are the USA, western Europe's Blue Banana and Japan.
The periphery supplies raw materials, food and cheap labour, with weak infrastructure and out-migration of people.
Most of sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Latin America and parts of South Asia are periphery.
The semi-periphery is made up of newly industrialised countries moving towards the core.
South Korea did so earlier; China, India, Brazil and Mexico are doing so now.
Britain industrialised first, from the late 18th century (the Industrial Revolution), followed by western Europe and the USA.
Colonial empires supplied the core with raw materials and markets, and profits were reinvested in the core.
Cumulative causation, a model by Gunnar Myrdal (1957): success attracts more investment, people and services, which increases success.
Backwash effects drain capital and skilled people from the periphery to the core.
The Blue Banana runs from south-east England and London through the Benelux countries and the Rhine valley to northern Italy (see the note 'Socio-economic regions').

notes.h: How the periphery developed, or failed to
points: Colonial economies were built around exporting one or two raw materials.
Railways ran from mines and plantations to ports, rather than linking regions to each other.
Borders were drawn by the colonisers.
After independence these economies depended on falling commodity prices, were burdened by debt and suffered conflict.
Spread effects and investment can raise peripheral regions.
The Asian Tigers and China moved from periphery to semi-periphery or core in about two generations.
Ireland moved from the European periphery to a core-like economy through MNC investment (see the note 'Irish Regions — Core and Peripheral').
The Brandt Line, from the Brandt Report of 1980, is a simple North–South model of the same pattern; criticism of it is in the note 'Option — Global Interdependence'.

notes.h: Sub-Saharan Africa: the main excluded region
notes.b: Sub-Saharan Africa is the main region excluded from world manufacturing. It has a very small share of world manufacturing and exports mostly unprocessed raw materials.
points: Nigeria: crude oil is most of its exports.
Zambia: copper is most of its exports.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo produces most of the world's cobalt and exports it raw despite its huge reserves, amid conflict.
Sudan: civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces since April 2023 has caused one of the world's largest displacement crises.
South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011, taking most of the oil fields.
The 2023 war is within Sudan, not a war with South Sudan.
Poor infrastructure: roads and ports are inadequate and electricity is unreliable.
Landlocked countries: Africa has 16, such as Chad, Niger, Mali and South Sudan, and they face high transport costs to reach ports.
Political instability, conflict and corruption scare off investment.
Low levels of education and skills, and poor health, limit the workforce.
Small, poor home markets give firms little reason to produce locally.
Heavy debt absorbs money that could fund development.
The colonial legacy: economies were set up to export raw materials, and that pattern persists.

Tariff escalation: rich countries charge higher tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials, so processing at home does not pay; coffee beans enter rich markets with low tariffs, while roasted coffee faces higher ones.
Competition from established Asian manufacturers, which already have supply chains and skilled workers.
Climate hazards such as drought reduce farm output and disrupt production.
The Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative, begun in 1996, gives debt relief through the World Bank and IMF.
The African Continental Free Trade Area began trading on 1 January 2021.
Chinese and other foreign investment is building infrastructure.
Fair trade (see the note 'Patterns in world trade').

notes.b: Globalisation is the growing integration of the world's economies through trade, investment, MNCs, technology and the movement of people and ideas.
points: About 80% of world trade is linked to the international production networks of MNCs (UNCTAD, 2013).
Much of it is intra-firm trade, between parts of the same company or with its suppliers in global value chains.
Trade is increasingly in components rather than finished goods.
Trade in services and digital trade has grown rapidly.
New trading powers, led by China, have entered world trade.
The WTO and trade blocs have lowered barriers.
Containerisation and huge ports have cut the cost of shipping.
E-commerce brings small sellers into world markets.
Consumers gain cheaper goods.
NICs and China gain jobs and growth.
Manufacturing regions in the core lose jobs.
Excluded regions fall further behind.
Workers in low-wage assembly can face poor and unsafe conditions, as the Rana Plaza collapse showed.
Transporting goods over long distances has environmental costs.
The US–China trade war from 2018, the US tariffs of 2025 and Brexit have raised barriers between major economies.
Governments are reshoring strategic industries such as chips, bringing production back home.
Supply-chain worries grew after COVID-19.

notes.b: India's economy was tightly controlled before 1991, and it opened to globalisation only after a crisis.
points: Five-year plans from 1951 directed investment and production.
Protection shielded Indian industries from foreign competition.
The Licence Raj: firms needed government licences to produce and expand, which limited competition and growth.
A balance-of-payments crisis in 1991 forced change.
Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh removed most licences, cut tariffs and opened India to foreign investment.

notes.b: Globalisation brought rapid growth, new industries and foreign investment.
points: Bengaluru became known as the 'Silicon Valley of India'.
IT and business-process outsourcing grew rapidly; Tata Consultancy Services (founded 1968), Infosys (founded 1981) and Wipro grew, with Bengaluru as a major hub.
Texas Instruments opened a design centre in Bengaluru in 1985.
Maruti Suzuki, a joint venture with Suzuki of Japan, made its first car in 1983.
India is a leading maker of generic medicines, earning it the name 'pharmacy of the world'.
Make in India, launched in 2014, aimed to attract manufacturing; iPhones are assembled near Chennai and Bengaluru (see the note 'One multinational company (MNC)').
Services produce over half of India's GDP, and India is among the world's five largest economies (early 2020s).
A growing middle class has emerged.
Hundreds of millions of people have been moved out of extreme poverty.
Inequality exists between cities and rural areas, and between states.
Small farmers are exposed to world prices.
Farmers' protests in 2020–21 were against three farm laws, which were repealed in November 2021.
Most workers are still in the informal sector.
Pollution and accidents at MNC plants: the Bhopal gas leak at the Union Carbide pesticide plant in December 1984 killed thousands; Union Carbide was a US MNC.
Reforms under Deng Xiaoping from 1978 opened China to foreign trade and investment.
Special Economic Zones from 1980 attracted foreign investment.
China joined the WTO on 11 December 2001.
China has been the largest goods exporter since 2009.
About 800 million people have been lifted out of extreme poverty since 1978 (World Bank).
Inequality exists between the coast and the interior.
Pollution from rapid industrial growth and dependence on exports are costs of this model.
Ready-made garments are most of Bangladesh's exports; it is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China.
The garment industry provides jobs, especially for women.
Rana Plaza, Savar, near Dhaka, collapsed on 24 April 2013, killing over 1,100 garment workers. It was a building collapse, not a fire.
The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh, signed in 2013 by clothing brands and unions, introduced factory inspections.

keyTerms.definition: A factory carrying out one stage of production, such as processing a raw material, making a component or assembling a product.
An area where firms import components and export finished goods free of customs duty, with tax breaks.
An assembly plant along Mexico's border with the USA that imports components duty-free and exports finished goods to the USA.
A wealthy, densely developed area with capital, MNC headquarters, research and development, and political power.
A poorer area that supplies raw materials, food and cheap labour, with weak infrastructure and out-migration.
Newly industrialised countries moving from the periphery towards the core.
The process by which success attracts more investment, people and services, which increases success further.
The draining of capital and skilled people from a periphery to a core.
A simple North–South division between the rich north and the poor south, proposed in the Brandt Report of 1980.
Higher tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials, which discourages processing in the exporting country.
Moving production back to the home country from abroad.
The growing integration of the world's economies through trade, investment, MNCs, technology and the movement of people and ideas.

questions.prompt: Explain the impact of globalisation on one developing economy that you have studied.
questions.model: India is the developing economy studied here. Before 1991 its economy was tightly controlled: five-year plans from 1951 directed investment, protection shielded Indian industries from foreign competition, and the Licence Raj required firms to hold government licences to produce and expand. A balance-of-payments crisis in 1991 forced change. Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh then removed most licences, cut tariffs and opened India to foreign investment. The positive impacts were rapid growth in IT and business-process outsourcing. Bengaluru, known as the Silicon Valley of India, became a hub for firms such as Tata Consultancy Services (founded 1968), Infosys (founded 1981) and Wipro, and Texas Instruments opened a design centre there in 1985. Foreign investment brought Maruti Suzuki, a joint venture with Suzuki of Japan, which made its first car in 1983. India became a leading maker of generic medicines and exports cars and pharmaceuticals. Make in India, launched in 2014, aimed to attract manufacturing, and iPhones are now assembled near Chennai and Bengaluru. Services produce over half of India's GDP, a growing middle class has emerged, and hundreds of millions of people have been moved out of extreme poverty. The negative impacts were serious too. Inequality exists between cities and rural areas and between states. Small farmers are exposed to world prices, which led to the farmers' protests of 2020–21 against three farm laws, repealed in November 2021. Most workers remain in the informal sector without security. Pollution and MNC accidents also occurred, as in the Bhopal gas leak at the Union Carbide pesticide plant in December 1984, which killed thousands. Overall, globalisation has brought growth and poverty reduction to India alongside inequality, insecure work and environmental harm.

questions.prompt: Examine why some regions of the world are excluded from world manufacturing activity.
questions.model: Sub-Saharan Africa is the main excluded region. It has a very small share of world manufacturing and exports mostly unprocessed raw materials: crude oil from Nigeria, copper from Zambia and cobalt from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Poor infrastructure, including roads, ports and unreliable electricity, raises the cost of producing and moving goods. Africa has 16 landlocked countries, such as Chad, Niger, Mali and South Sudan, which face high transport costs to reach ports. Political instability, conflict and corruption scare off investment; the civil war in Sudan since April 2023 is one example, and it has caused one of the world's largest displacement crises. Low levels of education, skills and health limit the workforce, and small, poor home markets give firms little reason to produce locally. Heavy debt absorbs money that could fund development. Tariff escalation means rich countries charge higher tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials: coffee beans enter rich markets with low tariffs, while roasted coffee faces higher ones, so processing at home does not pay. The colonial legacy left economies built around exporting raw materials, a pattern that persists. Competition from established Asian manufacturers, which already have supply chains and skilled workers, makes entry harder. Climate hazards such as drought reduce farm output. Responses include debt relief through the HIPC initiative from 1996, the African Continental Free Trade Area, which began trading on 1 January 2021, and foreign investment in infrastructure. Together these barriers explain why the region remains largely excluded from world manufacturing.

questions.prompt: Examine how globalisation has affected world trade.
questions.model: Globalisation is the growing integration of the world's economies through trade, investment, multinational companies (MNCs), technology and the movement of people and ideas. World trade has grown faster than output, and about 80% of it is linked to the international production networks of MNCs (UNCTAD, 2013). Much of it is intra-firm trade, between parts of the same company or with its suppliers in global value chains. Basic processing units are spread across countries: Nike designs and sells shoes from Beaverton, Oregon, while independent contract factories in Vietnam, China and Indonesia make them, and export processing zones such as Shannon Free Zone and the Shenzhen Special Economic Zone, as well as Mexico's maquiladoras, allow duty-free assembly for export. Trade is increasingly in components rather than finished goods, and trade in services and digital trade has grown rapidly. New trading powers, led by China, have entered world trade, and China has been the largest goods exporter since 2009. The WTO and trade blocs have lowered barriers, while containerisation and huge ports have cut shipping costs, and e-commerce brings small sellers into world markets. These changes have created winners and losers. Consumers gain cheaper goods, and NICs and China gain jobs and growth. Manufacturing regions in the core lose jobs, excluded regions fall further behind, and workers in low-wage assembly can face poor and unsafe conditions, as the Rana Plaza collapse of 2013 showed. Transport over long distances has environmental costs. In reaction, the US–China trade war from 2018, the US tariffs of 2025 and Brexit have raised barriers, and governments are reshoring strategic industries such as chips. Supply-chain worries grew after COVID-19. Globalisation has therefore increased world trade and linked economies closely, although much of that trade is controlled by MNCs and some regions have been left behind.
